title: Route53 — DNS & Routing
subtitle: Domain registration, DNS records, health checks, and intelligent traffic routing across regions

content.text: Route53 is AWS's DNS service and domain registrar. It resolves domain names to IP addresses with 100% SLA uptime — the only AWS service with this guarantee. Beyond basic DNS, Route53 supports intelligent routing: send 10% of traffic to a new version (weighted routing), route users to the closest region (latency-based routing), or fail over to a backup when the primary is down (failover routing).
DNS record types — the essential ones

content.code:
A RECORD      → Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address
  example.com → 1.2.3.4

AAAA RECORD   → Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address
  example.com → 2001:db8::1

CNAME         → Maps a hostname to another hostname (canonical name)
  www.example.com → example.com
  Cannot use CNAME at the zone apex (example.com itself — use ALIAS)
  Cannot use CNAME for the root domain

ALIAS         → AWS-specific, like CNAME but works at zone apex
  example.com → d123.cloudfront.net    ✓ works
  example.com → my-alb.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com  ✓ works
  Free of charge (no query charges for ALIAS records)
  Auto-updates if target IP changes

MX RECORD     → Mail server for the domain
  example.com → 10 mail.example.com (priority 10)

TXT RECORD    → Text data — domain verification, SPF/DKIM for email
  example.com → 'v=spf1 include:mailgun.org ~all'

NS RECORD     → Which nameservers are authoritative for the domain
  Set automatically by Route53 when you create a hosted zone

SOA RECORD    → Start of Authority — metadata about the zone

content.text: Setting up a domain in Route53

content.code:
SIMPLE:          Single record, one destination (default)
  api.myapp.com → 1.2.3.4

WEIGHTED:        Distribute traffic by percentage
  api.myapp.com → 1.2.3.4 (weight 90)  ← v1 (90% of traffic)
  api.myapp.com → 5.6.7.8 (weight 10)  ← v2 canary (10% of traffic)
  Use: canary deployments, A/B testing

LATENCY-BASED:   Route to the lowest-latency region for each user
  api.myapp.com → ALB in us-east-1    (for North American users)
  api.myapp.com → ALB in ap-south-1   (for Asian users)
  api.myapp.com → ALB in eu-west-1    (for European users)
  Use: global applications, latency-sensitive APIs

FAILOVER:        Primary/secondary with health check
  api.myapp.com → Primary (health check every 30s)
  api.myapp.com → Secondary (only used if primary fails health check)
  Use: disaster recovery, active-passive HA

GEOLOCATION:     Route based on user's geographic location
  api.myapp.com → EU endpoint  (for EU users — GDPR compliance)
  api.myapp.com → US endpoint  (for US users)
  Use: data sovereignty, language/content routing

MULTI-VALUE:     Return multiple IPs, DNS-level load balancing
  Returns up to 8 healthy IPs — client picks one
  Use: simple round-robin without a load balancer

content.text: Health checks make your routing intelligent. Attach a Route53 health check to your records. Route53 pings your endpoint every 10-30 seconds. If it fails 3 consecutive checks, Route53 automatically removes that record from DNS responses. Combined with failover routing, this gives you automatic DNS-level failover when a region goes down.

questions.question: You want to route users in India to an API server in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) and users in the US to us-east-1 (Virginia), to minimize latency. Which Route53 routing policy should you use?
options: Geolocation routing — route based on the user's country
Latency-based routing — automatically routes each user to the lowest-latency region
Weighted routing — send 50% of traffic to each region
Failover routing — primary in one region, backup in another
questions.explanation: Latency-based routing is the right choice. It measures actual network latency between the user and each configured region, then routes to the fastest one. Unlike geolocation (which routes by country and may not reflect actual latency), latency-based routing dynamically optimizes for real network conditions. If a user in India has better latency to Singapore than Mumbai on a given day, latency routing would correctly route them to Singapore.

faq.q: Should I register my domain in Route53 or another registrar?
faq.a: Registering in Route53 is convenient — DNS is set up automatically, renewals are managed in AWS, and you can use ALIAS records at the apex. Cost is competitive (~$12/year for .com). But if you have an existing registrar you prefer, you can keep the domain there and just use Route53 for DNS by updating the nameservers to Route53's NS records. Most teams eventually consolidate to Route53 for simplicity.

examples: Netflix uses latency-based routing to serve content from the nearest region. During a US-East-1 incident in 2012, failover routing would have redirected traffic to EU/US-West — they've since built this capability
Weighted routing with 1%/99% split is how teams do canary deployments at the DNS level — expose 1% of users to a new version, monitor error rates, then gradually increase the weight to 100%
